寶石角笛主要作為牧人樂器，十五世紀已在歐洲使用，出土實例見於義大利、匈牙利與德國: The gemshorn served mainly as a shepherd's instrument and was in use in Europe by the fifteenth century, with excavated examples from Italy, Hungary and Germany; one complete clay instrument, buried under the foundations of a house in 145, can be dated at least to that year. Its early history is unknown; it is illustrated in the 1485 Dance of Death and in Sebastian Virdung's book of 1511, and Scottish documents also call it the “goat horn”. It grew rarer after the middle of the sixteenth century and was taken up again in the early-music revival of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Horace Fitzpatrick adopted recorder fingering and developed a consort family, and from the 1960s it has been widely popular.
寶石角笛是歐洲氣鳴樂器，屬卵形笛家族，H-S 編號 421.221.4。傳統以岩: The gemshorn is a European aerophone of the ovoid-flute family, H-S number 421.221.4. Traditionally it was made from the horn of a chamois, a goat or another animal; today cow horn is common. The hollow horn has fingerholes on the front, the tip is kept as the bottom, and the wide end carries a wooden fipple and a recorder-style window, so it sounds by blowing and covering the holes. Its timbre is close to a flute but with fewer overtones. It was in use by the fifteenth century, mainly as a pastoral instrument.
寶石角笛的音色接近其他笛類，但泛音較少，近似陶笛。其發聲依靠寬端裝入的哨嘴栓與正: The gemshorn sounds close to other flutes but with fewer overtones, rather like an ocarina. It sounds through the fipple plug fitted into the wide end and the window on the front face, and opening and closing the holes sets the pitch. Sixteenth-century images show early instruments with few holes and a limited range; the fifteenth-century clay example has a chromatic octave. Modern makers often use Baroque recorder fingering. The source mentions no means of controlling volume; a tuning ring, or wax partly closing the thumbhole at the back, can lower the fundamental by about a major second, which is a change of pitch rather than of volume.
寶石角笛舊時以岩羚羊、山羊或其他適合動物的角製成；現存十五世紀完整器有陶土製。現: The gemshorn was formerly made from the horn of a chamois, a goat or another suitable animal; the complete fifteenth-century example that survives is of fired clay. Today cow horn is mostly used, because it is easy to obtain and does not endanger wild animals. A wooden fipple plug fits into the wide end and recorder-style fingerholes are cut on the front; on more advanced instruments a metal tuning ring sits between the window and the top fingerhole, and the thumbhole can be partly closed with wax for tuning. There are also versions in synthetic materials or wood.
